episode_title: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate

stories.topic: Larry White and the Forgotten World of Free Banking
stories.summary: Amit recently recorded a Seen and the Unseen episode with Larry White, author of 'The Clash of Economic Ideas' and a world expert on free banking. White's research showed that in many historical periods, instead of one official central-bank currency, multiple banks issued competing currencies and the system worked 'marvelously well.' Larry was also cited by some of the early crypto pioneers (including possible Satoshi Nakamoto candidates) before cryptocurrency was even born.
stories.insight: What feels self-evident, like the state's monopoly on issuing currency, often isn't natural at all. When you take an institution for granted, the cure is to look at history: someone, somewhere, has tried the alternative, and the results are usually more interesting than the orthodoxy admits.

stories.topic: Subramaniam Swami's Plan to Make the Rupee Equal the Dollar
stories.summary: About 12-13 years ago, when the BJP was in opposition and the rupee was at 40-50 to the dollar, their adviser Subramaniam Swami insisted the right level was 1 rupee = 1 dollar. The party-in-opposition campaigned on bringing the number down. Now in power, with the rupee at 80, the same rhetoric is being thrown back at them.
stories.insight: Currency rhetoric is one of the purest examples of innumerate nationalism. The number on the screen says nothing about national strength: Japan has 130 yen to the dollar and is one of the most successful countries in the world. 'Stronger' and 'weaker' are unit-dependent talk masquerading as economics.

stories.topic: The Reliance Benzene Ship and Korean Prices
stories.summary: Ajay was on the board of a company that bought benzene from Reliance's Jamnagar refinery. Every day, one ship of benzene crossed the Gulf of Gujarat between two Indian parties, and yet the price was set as the Korean price of benzene multiplied by the rupee-dollar exchange rate. There was a daily fluctuation built into a purely Indian transaction.
stories.insight: Import parity pricing means the exchange rate reaches into every domestic transaction in any globally-traded commodity. Even when the producer and buyer are both Indian, using Indian inputs and Indian labour, the LME or Korean price multiplied by USD/INR controls the day's bargain. The currency is not a niche concern of importers and exporters; it is everywhere.

stories.topic: Yom Kippur and the Instant Price of Crude Oil
stories.summary: When Ajay was very young, OPEC quadrupled the price of crude oil from 2 dollars to 8 dollars after the Yom Kippur War. He recalls screaming with laughter at people who said 'but the high-priced oil hasn't reached India yet, so why has the local price already gone up?' His point: the price changes the moment information arrives, not when the ship docks. The barrel of oil already in the tank does not have a label saying 'purchased at the old price.'
stories.insight: Markets price on information, not on physical inventory. Once new information arrives, every existing unit of the commodity is repriced instantaneously, because the alternative is for an arbitrageur to make free money. This is one of the more counter-intuitive truths of how prices propagate.

stories.topic: George Soros vs. The Bank of England
stories.summary: Once upon a time, the Bank of England tried to distort the currency market and hold the pound at an artificial level. George Soros understood the position correctly, had the courage of his convictions, and placed an enormous bet that the Bank of England would not be able to maintain its target. He won; the bank capitulated.
stories.insight: When a central bank fights a market it is fundamentally wrong about, even one informed individual with conviction can outweigh state power. Sustained currency manipulation is not just bad economics; it is an offer of free money to anyone willing to take the other side.

stories.topic: The 1966 Devaluation and the Oil Shock
stories.summary: Indira Gandhi's 1966 rupee devaluation was unpopular and is usually judged by what happened in 1967, 1968, 1969 — when the impact looks underwhelming. Ajay argues this misreads the time lag. Large exchange-rate movements take years to flow through to imports and exports, and by the time the early-70s oil shock hit, India's tradables had already adjusted. The much-derided devaluation was an important reason India weathered the oil shock relatively well.
stories.insight: Macroeconomic causes and effects are separated by years; judging a policy by its 12-month optics is almost guaranteed to give the wrong answer. Most disasters and most rescues are slow.

stories.topic: Ashok Desai and the Generational Young-Turk Idea
stories.summary: Ashok Desai, who drafted Manmohan Singh's July 1991 budget speech, once told Ajay: 'In my generation, the young-Turk idea was openness to international trade — we make fun of our ancestors for trade barriers. In your generation, the young-Turk idea is exchange-rate flexibility and openness on the capital account. I see that look in your eyes when I talk about restrictions, and I know what you're thinking — what's wrong with this guy.'
stories.insight: Reform is a relay race, not a finish. Each generation extends the consensus by one notch and is then politely scoffed at by the next. The honest stance is to recognise this in advance: whatever feels too radical to your elders is probably what your descendants will take for granted.

stories.topic: Ajay's Plan to Change the Country
stories.summary: Many months ago, by the seaside, Amit asked Ajay what his plan was. Ajay said with full stops and an exclamation mark: 'Desh badalna hai.' Amit replied: 'Bro, desh nahin badlega.' Ajay insisted, 'Desh badalna hai.' Amit asked, 'Socho, badla kab tak?' After a pause, Ajay said something to the effect of 'It will take time.' Amit's answer: 'Don't worry, YouTube karte hai.' That is the origin of Everything is Everything.
stories.insight: Small projects with grand ambitions usually start as a private vow on a beach. The bridge between 'desh badalna hai' and actually changing anything is not policy power but persistent, patient communication — show up every Friday and try to shape the next generation.

stories.topic: The Show-Notes Mistake That Will Live in Infamy
stories.summary: Three or four episodes ago, Amit asked Ajay to send a list of his favourite papers for the show notes. Ajay sent them at the last minute, and Amit cut-pasted at 2:30am. In one entry, Ajay had written 'Abhijit Banerjee' as a co-author of his misinvoicing paper. The actual co-author is Abhijit Sen Gupta. Someone caught it. Amit, who prides himself on his show notes, recounts the wound with comic indignation: 'The one time there was a mistake in Everything is Everything show notes, it was because of this shabby fool.'
stories.insight: A small, warming reminder that even the most careful operations have a single point of failure — usually a tired collaborator at 2:30am. Owning the mistake (and good-naturedly blaming someone else) is part of the show's charm.

recommendations.item: Larry White and the First Principles of Money (Episode 397, The Seen and the Unseen)

recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive Seen and the Unseen episode with the world expert on free banking, who has rewritten Amit's intuitions about state monopolies on currency.
recommendations.reason: If you want to break the assumption that currency must be issued by a single central bank, this is the conversation. White is also cited in the early-crypto literature, and this is the gateway to that whole intellectual lineage.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence H. White
recommendations.context: Larry White's history of the major debates in economic thought.
recommendations.reason: A serious, historically-grounded survey of how economic ideas have battled each other across the twentieth century, by someone who has lived inside the free-banking debate.

recommendations.item: Free Banking in Britain: Theory, Experience, and Debate, 1800-1845
recommendations.creator: Lawrence H. White
recommendations.context: White's foundational work documenting an extended historical period in which competing private banks issued their own currencies.
recommendations.reason: The empirical backbone for the case that competitive issuance of currency is not a thought experiment but a real, working system from history. The book that quietly laid groundwork for crypto.

recommendations.context: Amit and Ajay's new online course launching with five Saturdays of webinars in November 2024 — three sessions per Saturday.

core_ideas.concept: The Exchange Rate Is the Most Important Price
core_ideas.explanation: All international trade is intermediated by the exchange rate, so importers and exporters live by it. But beyond direct trade, every globally-traded commodity (steel, benzene, oil) is priced as the global price multiplied by the exchange rate — even in purely Indian transactions between Indian buyers and Indian sellers. And on top of trade sits finance, which today is vastly larger than trade and equally driven by the currency. The exchange rate touches almost every economic transaction, often invisibly.
core_ideas.quote: The exchange rate is the most important price of the economy. — Josh Felman

core_ideas.concept: Strong and Weak Are Meaningless Words
core_ideas.explanation: There is no relationship between the numerical level of a country's exchange rate and its national success. Japan trades at 130 yen to the dollar and is one of the most successful countries on earth. If India redenominated tomorrow so that 1 rupee became 10 new rupees, the rupee-dollar number would jump from 80 to 800 and absolutely nothing real would change. The level of the exchange rate is just a unit, like measuring height in millimetres versus inches.
core_ideas.quote: It's as silly as counting my height in millimeters versus my height in inches and getting excited.

core_ideas.explanation: For globally-traded commodities, there is no separate Indian or Chinese market — there is one world market with one price (e.g. the LME price of steel). The local price in any country is the global price multiplied by the exchange rate. The implication is profound: even purely domestic transactions, between Indian producers using Indian labour, electricity and ore, are priced at the global price times the rupee-dollar rate. A currency depreciation is a windfall for these producers because their costs are unchanged but their rupee revenue rises directly into operating profit.

There is no central planner setting one global steel price; it emerges from thousands of arbitrageurs watching the price in Singapore vs Dubai vs Vishakapatnam, ready to buy in one place and ship to another the moment a gap opens. Most people don't bother arbitraging — they take the global price as given — because a tiny number of professionals make sure any deviation is immediately closed. This is how the world organises itself into one price for one good without anybody coordinating it.
core_ideas.quote: The chains of arbitrage hold prices together.

core_ideas.concept: Prices Move on Information, Not on Inventory
core_ideas.explanation: When OPEC raised the crude price from 2 to 8 dollars after Yom Kippur, the price in California and India jumped immediately — long before the new ship of expensive crude actually arrived. The barrel already in the tank has no label saying it was bought at the old price. The instant new information arrives, every existing unit is repriced; otherwise an arbitrageur would buy out the inventory and resell at the new price for free. Markets are information machines, not physical-flow machines.

core_ideas.concept: Three Rooms in the House (Exchange-Rate Regimes)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's three-case taxonomy: Room 1 is North Korea, where every single currency transaction has the state as one counterparty and private exchanges are violently suppressed. Room 2 is India, where private-to-private transactions are allowed but heavily restricted, intermediated through banks, and the central bank actively manipulates the rate. Room 3 is the advanced economies — US, UK, most of Europe — where the central bank does no trading on the currency market and the rate is whatever the market decides. Understanding which room a country is in is essential to understanding its economy.
core_ideas.quote: These are three rooms in the house... For each country, to understand a country, you must understand its exchange-rate regime.

core_ideas.concept: Floating Exchange Rates as Automatic Macroeconomic Stabilisers
core_ideas.explanation: When things go badly in a country (floods, collapse of law and order, demonetisation), exports fail to deliver and capital takes flight, so the currency depreciates. Depreciation does three good things automatically: it makes exports more competitive abroad, it boosts the operating profits of all import-parity-priced producers, and it makes imports costlier so domestic substitutes pick up demand. In good times the reverse happens — appreciation cools an overheating economy. Floating exchange rates deliver macroeconomic stabilisation through the price system, with no policymaker required.
core_ideas.quote: Floating exchange rates stabilize the economy. They are a shock absorber.

core_ideas.concept: The Closet Bureaucrat in Each of Us
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's diagnosis of the Indian elite's irrational love of exchange-rate fixedness: there is a closet bureaucrat inside each of us that wants a simple, unchanging life. We have accepted that the price of steel and cement and nickel must fluctuate, that we live in a market economy where running a business means constantly reshaping in response to changing prices. But for some reason we still want one price — the exchange rate — to stand still. It is the same instinct that makes top-down planning emotionally appealing.
core_ideas.quote: I think there's a closet bureaucrat inside each of us that just wants a simple unchanging life.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framing: every voluntary transaction between two people leaves both better off — it is a positive-sum game, a 'double thank you' moment. Restrictions on cross-border transactions don't merely tax those exchanges; they prevent them from happening at all, destroying the value that would have been created. Worse, the apparatus to enforce restrictions (banks, lawyers, accountants, the Enforcement Directorate) extracts further rent from those who do transact. The state is not just stealing from the people; it is burning value that nobody ever gets to taste.

core_ideas.concept: FERA, FEMA and the Inverted Default
core_ideas.explanation: FERA (1973) made foreign-exchange transactions criminal, including possession of dollar bills. FEMA (1999) replaced it but the criminal clauses returned in 2015. Most damningly, FEMA opens with the proposition that all cross-border activities are banned except when permitted by the law — then proceeds to enumerate exceptions. Any sensible legal regime should invert this: freedom is the default, restrictions are exceptions. India's approach amounts to a permanent employment-guarantee programme for lawyers and accountants who shepherd routine transactions through hundreds of circulars, notifications and thousands of cases.
core_ideas.quote: Freedom should be the norm. And maybe you have some exceptions, and we can debate what the exceptions should be.

core_ideas.concept: The Implementation Gap of the 1991 Reforms
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's broader critique of the 1991 generation: they had economics, but they did not have public administration, law, or public-choice theory. They believed that 'people like me will be running these organisations and how can it go bad? Because I'm a good guy.' So they gave the RBI and the ED arbitrary powers, assuming benevolent technocrats would always be in charge. The same mistake Nehru's generation made with the constitution — protecting the state from the people instead of the people from the state. Real reform needs economics married to skeptical institutional design.

The Enforcement Directorate, which enforces FEMA, has draconian powers including the right to conduct raids — politely called 'search and seizure' in government. Pre-dawn knocks on the door, people made to sit while documents are demanded, all under a poorly-drafted law with little rule-of-law oversight. Many political actors today understand the ED is dangerous; the economists who wrote FEMA and built the ED did not anticipate this, because they assumed they would always be the ones holding the powers.

core_ideas.concept: Misinvoicing as De Facto Capital-Account Convertibility
core_ideas.explanation: Inside India's nominally closed capital account, vast capital flows happen through misinvoicing — an Indian company invoicing a 100-rupee shipment as 10, so 90 rupees stays abroad as a private capital outflow, or vice versa. Ajay, Ila Patnaik and Abhijit Sen Gupta measured the magnitudes; they are 'staggering' and dwarf the formal capital-account flows. The lesson: a state cannot actually squash freedom enough to choke off cross-border activity. It just shifts that activity into illegality, where it benefits the rich and the connected and harasses everyone else.

core_ideas.concept: Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's preferred reform philosophy, lifted from Deng. You cannot dismantle the edifice of central planning in one sweeping change; you must remove one regulation, one law at a time, persuading many people that this particular regulation makes no sense. That requires teams of full-time researchers, deep data work, conversations with practitioners, blog posts, videos, and patient persuasion. India had this knowledge community once; it does not today. Until it is rebuilt, no significant exchange-rate reform is possible.

core_ideas.concept: The Generational Relay Race of Reform
core_ideas.explanation: Captured in Ashok Desai's anecdote: each generation has a young-Turk idea that scandalises the previous one and is taken for granted by the next. For Desai's 1991 generation it was openness to international trade. For Ajay's generation it is exchange-rate flexibility and openness on the capital account. By the time these become consensus, the next generation will be impatient with us about something we cannot yet see.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Targeting as the Foundation Stone
core_ideas.explanation: One thing in India is genuinely in good shape: the Reserve Bank of India has been given a clear, narrow mandate to deliver an inflation target rather than to manage the exchange rate. This is the right division of labour: the central bank should be accountable for one thing it can actually deliver. The concrete has been poured on this foundation. What remains is to clear away the rubble of FEMA and the Enforcement Directorate sitting on top of it.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's redenomination thought experiment: 'Imagine the government announces all old rupees become 10 new rupees. INR goes from 80 to the dollar to 800. Did anything change? No, nothing changes. People who live in a country called millimeter must be feeling damn jealous of people who live in a country called inch.'
Amit on Ajay's bumper-sticker for Tata Steel's logo: 'From iron ore to I-on-or — yes, they've moved a distance.'

Ajay on the source of high India steel prices: 'The blood relatives of Rabindranath Tagore are engaged in the highly intellectual activity of watching the price of steel in Singapore.' (As an example of Bengali arbitrageurs.) Self-deprecating in-joke he revisits when Amit says 'I can see the skeptical Bengali saying no no no, in everything else markets are good but exchange rates should be fixed' and Ajay corrects: 'Skeptical Bengali in nothing! In everything markets are good.'
Amit, on financial wonkery: 'A lot of people think this is wonks talking wonkery, doesn't really affect us. No man — this shit has humanitarian consequences.'

Amit, after Ajay's address to the elite: 'I will apologize that you are not necessarily the elite of India... You include the dentists of Connecticut and Kyoto. You include the grandmothers of Connecticut and Kyoto. If you happen to be a grandmother and a dentist at the same time and live dual lives in Connecticut and Kyoto, come to our website.'
Amit on Ajay's cinema-watching habits: 'Ajay has watched twenty films in twenty years. Eleven of them are The Matrix.'
Amit's request to listeners about the next episode: 'Take your time, watch it at 0.25x so it lasts and lasts and lasts till we get there.'

Ajay's cat is named FEMA. Or, as Ajay claims after Amit raises an eyebrow about the name, 'femur' — supposedly because the cat had a fall from a third-floor house. The cover story does not appear to convince Amit.
Ila Patnaik on Ajay: 'Ajay is a one-track mind. All he thinks about is exchange rates.'
Bob Dylan: 'He not busy being born is busy dying.' Amit's go-to opener for episodes about questioning what we take for granted.
Jadi Tata on Nehru: Nehru once said to JRD Tata, 'Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.' Amit's shorthand for the philosophical wrongness of Nehruvian economics.
Subramaniam Swami's claim that the rupee should equal the dollar at a 1:1 exchange rate. The canonical example of currency-level innumeracy in Indian political discourse.

George Soros breaking the Bank of England — the most famous one-man-against-the-state currency story, invoked as a parable of why central banks should not pretend they can hold a market rate against fundamentals.

Black Wednesday-era Bretton Woods architecture — Keynes the architect, Nixon the executioner. Ajay frames the post-1971 world of fiat currencies as the logical consequence of Bretton Woods having always been an unwise design.
'Desh badlana hai' — Ajay's seaside vow that Amit met with 'desh nahin badlega'. The line has become the unofficial origin myth of Everything is Everything. (Amit's resolution: 'YouTube karte hai.')
